source_text:
Ὥστε οὖν, ἀδελφοι μου, ἀγωνισώμεθα εἰδότες, ὅτι ἐν χερσὶν ὁ ἀγὼν καὶ ὅτι εἰς τοὺς φθαρτοὺς ἀγῶνας καταπλέουσα: πολλοί, ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντες στεφανοῦνται, εἰ μὴ οἱ πολλὰ κοπιάσαντες καὶ καλῶς ἀγωνισάμενοι.
ἡμεῖς οὖν ἀγωνισώμεθα, ἵνα πάντες στεφανωθῶμεν.
ὥστε θέωμεν τὴν ὁδὸν τὴν εὐθείαν, ἀγῶνα τὸν ἄφθαρτον, καὶ πολλοὶ εἰς αὐτὸν καταπλεύσωμεν καὶ ἀγωνισώμεθα, ἵνα καὶ στεφανωθῶμεν: καὶ εἰ μὴ δυνάμεθα πάντες στεφανωθῆναι, κἂν ἐγγὺς τοῦ στεφάνου γενώμεθα.
εἰδέναι ἡμᾶς δεῖ, ὅτι ὁ τὸν φθαρτὸν ἀγῶνα ἀγωνιζόμενος, ἐὰν εὑρεθῇ φθείρων, μαστιγωθεὶς αἴρεται καὶ ἔξω βάλλεται τοῦ σταδίου.
τί δοκεῖτε; ὁ τὸν τῆς ἀφθαρσίας ἀγῶνα φθείρας τί παθεῖται;
τῶν γὰρ μὴ τηρησάντων, φησίν, τὴν σφραγῖδα ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν οὐ τελευτήσει καὶ τὸ πῦρ αὐτῶν οὐ σβεσθήσεται, καὶ ἔσονται εἰς ὅρασιν πάσῃ σαρκί.
orientation: The preacher is exhorting the congregation to strive in the contest of faith, comparing earthly athletic contests with the imperishable contest and warning of punishment for corrupting it.
pass_a_gloss: So then, my brothers, let us contend knowing that in [our] hands [is] the contest and that into the perishable contests many sail in, but not all are crowned, except those who have labored much and contended well. We therefore let us contend, in order that all may be crowned. So let us run the straight road, the imperishable contest, and let many sail into it and let us contend, in order that also we may be crowned; and if we are not able all to be crowned, at least let us come near to the crown. [It is] necessary [for] us to know that the one contending in the perishable contest, if he is found corrupting [it], having been scourged is taken up and thrown outside of the stadium. What do you think? The one who has corrupted the contest of immortality, what will he suffer? For of those who have not kept, he says, the seal, their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched, and they will be for a spectacle to all flesh.

choices.why: Keeps the athletic-contest metaphor explicit; 'strive' would lose the agonistic register.
The verb means to sail into harbor; the image is of many entering the contest, so 'sail in' preserves the nautical metaphor.
The glossary bans 'incorruption' for ἀφθαρσία; for the adjective, 'imperishable' is the natural English and matches the contrast with 'perishable.'
The verb φθείρω means to corrupt or ruin; 'corrupted' keeps the root connection with 'perishable' and 'imperishable.'

choices.english: for a spectacle to all flesh
choices.why: The phrase means they will be seen by all flesh; 'spectacle' captures the public display of judgment, and 'flesh' follows the glossary.
rejected: for a sight to all flesh
to be seen by all flesh

bible_refs.note: ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν οὐ τελευτήσει καὶ τὸ πῦρ αὐτῶν οὐ σβεσθήσεται, καὶ ἔσονται εἰς ὅρασιν πάσῃ σαρκί

pass_b_english: So then, my brothers, let us enter the struggle, knowing that the contest is at hand. In perishable contests many enter, but not all are crowned. Only those who have labored much and contended well receive the crown.
Let us therefore contend, so that all of us may be crowned.

Let us run the straight course, the imperishable contest. Let many of us sail into it and contend, so that we may also be crowned. And if we cannot all be crowned, let us at least come near the crown.
We must understand this: the one who contends in a perishable contest, if he is found cheating, is scourged, removed, and thrown out of the stadium.
What do you think? What will the one who has corrupted the contest of immortality suffer?
For of those who have not kept the seal, Scripture says, "Their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched, and they will be a spectacle to all flesh."

problems.quote: the contest is at hand and that many sail in to the perishable contests
problems.why: Source says the contest is at hand AND that [the church?] sails into perishable contests; English merges and loses the separate clause.
problems.fix: the contest is at hand and that she sails into the perishable contests
problems.ruling: Source has two clauses: ὅτι ἐν χερσὶν ὁ ἀγὼν (contest is at hand) AND ὅτι εἰς τοὺς φθαρτοὺς ἀγῶνας καταπλέουσα (that [we/one] sail into perishable contests). English 'many sail in to' incorrectly merges into second clause, losing the separate subject and making 'many' the subject of sailing. The participial clause καταπλέουσα has no expressed subject in Greek; English supplies 'many' and loses the two distinct ὅτι clauses, changing syntax and meaning.

problems.why: 'αἴρεται' here means 'is removed/taken away' (passive), not 'taken up' which suggests elevation or rescue; in context of scourging and ejection, 'removed' or 'carried off'
problems.fix: scourged, removed, and thrown out of the stadium
problems.ruling: αἴρεται here means 'is removed/taken away' for ejection; 'taken up' wrongly suggests elevation or rescue, misleading readers.

problems.fix: many, but not all, are crowned—only those who have labored much and contended well
problems.ruling: πολλοί ('many') is omitted; source says 'many, but not all are crowned,' English drops the initial πολλοί, changing meaning.

edits.new: many, but not all, are crowned—only those who have labored much and contended well.

problems.quote: she sails into the perishable contests
problems.why: Feminine participle refers to 'contest' (ἀγών), not a person; 'she' is nonsensical.

problems.quote: many, but not all, are crowned
problems.why: Missing 'only' (εἰ μὴ); Greek says 'many, but not all are crowned—only those who...'
problems.fix: many, but not all, are crowned—only those who have labored much and contended well
problems.ruling: εἰ μὴ οἱ πολλὰ κοπιάσαντες is omitted; 'only those who labored much' restricts who among the many are crowned.

fixed: The second problem is not real: the English already includes 'only' in 'only those who have labored much and contended well', matching the Greek εἰ μὴ.

problems.quote: knowing that the contest is at hand and that it sails into the perishable contests, many, but not all, are crowned
problems.why: Sentence is incoherent; 'it sails into' makes no sense here.
problems.fix: Reconstruct: 'knowing that the contest is at hand, and that in perishable contests many contend but not all are crowned.'

problems.quote: the imperishable contest, and let many of us sail into it and contend
problems.why: 'Sail into it' is nonsensical for a contest metaphor.
problems.fix: Replace 'sail into it' with 'enter it' or 'engage in it.'

problems.quote: Brothers and sisters, this is how we ought to think about Jesus Christ
problems.why: The congregation is addressed inconsistently; reader may wonder if different groups are being addressed.
problems.fix: Standardize to 'brothers and sisters' throughout, or note that 'brothers' is inclusive.

edits.old: knowing that the contest is at hand and that it sails into the perishable contests, many, but not all, are crowned—only those who have labored much and contended well.

fixed: The glossary problem about 'brothers and sisters' is not a real problem in this passage; the source uses 'brothers' (ἀδελφοί μου), and the English correctly renders it as 'my brothers.' No change needed.

problems.why: The congregation is addressed with three different forms; a reader may wonder if different groups or tones are intended.
problems.fix: Standardize to one form throughout, or note that all forms address the same congregation.

problems.quote: In perishable contests many sail in
problems.why: 'Sail in' is an odd rendering; the Greek likely refers to athletes entering a contest, not sailing.

problems.quote: Their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched, and they will be a spectacle to all flesh.
problems.why: The first two clauses are from Isaiah 66:24, but 'a spectacle to all flesh' is not in Isaiah; it may conflate Isaiah with another source.
problems.fix: Note the first two clauses are Isaiah 66:24; 'spectacle to all flesh' is from another source.

edits.old: In perishable contests many sail in

fixed: Brothers: The source uses ἀδελφοί μου (my brothers), a standard address to the congregation; no change needed.
Sail in: The Greek καταπλέουσα means 'sail in,' but in context it refers to entering a contest; 'enter' is clearer and still faithful.

Scripture: The first two clauses are from Isaiah 66:24; 'a spectacle to all flesh' is not from Isaiah but is part of the author's own expansion. The English correctly renders the source, so no change needed.

problems.why: Same audience addressed with different forms; reader may wonder if subgroups are meant.
problems.fix: Use one consistent form of address throughout.

problems.why: Multiple terms for the same concept without clear signposting; reader may lose the thread.
problems.fix: Clarify that all terms refer to one spiritual contest vs. athletic ones.

problems.why: 'Sail in' does not fit an athletic contest metaphor; likely a mistranslation of a word meaning 'compete' or 'enter'.

variants.text: Let many of us sail into it

edits.old: In perishable contests many sail in

fixed: The source uses ἀδελφοί μου ('my brothers'), and the English 'my brothers' is consistent with the brief's voice and glossary; no change needed.
The source distinguishes the perishable contest (φθαρτοὺς ἀγῶνας) from the imperishable contest (ἀγῶνα τὸν ἄφθαρτον), and the English already marks this contrast clearly; no change needed.

The source καταπλέουσα means 'sail in' (literally 'sail down into'), but the English 'sail in' is awkward for an athletic contest; 'enter' better conveys the sense of competing in the perishable contests.

polish.changed: Clarified the contest metaphor by separating the opening sentence into two coherent statements, removed the nonsensical 'sails into' phrasing for entering a contest, and set the final Scripture quotation apart with quotation marks while preserving every claim and reference.

dismissed.quote: it sails into the perishable contests
dismissed.why: Subject confusion: 'it sails' makes 'contest' the subject, but Greek likely means 'we sail into' or 'many sail into'; the participle's subject is unclear but context demands 'we' or 'many'.
dismissed.note: Stale: the quoted text is not in the current English, which already reads 'many sail in' (standard emendation καταπλέουσι πολλοί).

dismissed.quote: the one who has corrupted the contest of immortality
dismissed.why: Tense/aspect error: aorist participle 'φθείρας' means 'having corrupted' or 'who corrupts', but 'has corrupted' suggests completed action; more importantly, the question asks what he WILL suffer, implying future consequence for present/future corruption.
dismissed.note: Aorist participle 'has corrupted' vs 'corrupts' is style.

dismissed.quote: let many of us sail into it
dismissed.why: Wrong subject: 'many of us' but Greek uses hortative subjunctive 'let us sail', calling all to action, not just many.
dismissed.note: Stale quote (English now 'let many of us enter it'); πολλοὶ ... καταπλεύσωμεν = 'let us, many of us, sail in', so the English is right and checker's reading drops πολλοί.
